title: Open Quantum Systems Toolkit
intro: A quantum reservoir is an open quantum system driven by data: each input step is a channel, its memory is the way that channel forgets, and its output is a noisy estimate of expectation values. This chapter teaches the open-system toolkit that the rest of the shelf uses, in four lessons, starting from the density matrix.

blocks.text: A first course in quantum computing describes a closed system: a state vector that a unitary matrix rotates. That picture cannot describe a reservoir computer, for a simple reason. A unitary never loses information: two runs that start differently stay exactly as distinguishable as they were, for ever. A reservoir has to do the opposite. After a long stream of inputs, its state must depend on the recent inputs and not on how it was started; this is the echo state property, introduced for classical networks in The Echo State Property (#/qrc/foundations/echo-state-property). Forgetting means discarding information, and in quantum mechanics that means coupling to something you then ignore: an environment that leaks energy, a qubit that is reset to carry the next input, a measurement whose result is thrown away. So every working quantum reservoir is an open system, whether the openness is engineered, natural or comes from the readout.

This chapter gives you the language to describe all three, and the tools to answer the questions a designer asks: how much does one step forget, how long does the memory last, and what does it cost to read the answer out? It assumes the Quantum Mechanics shelf up to Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states) and the chapter Getting Started (#/qrc/start), especially A Quantum Reservoir Worked by Hand (#/qrc/start/quantum-reservoir-by-hand), which pushes a two-qubit reservoir through three steps by hand; the lessons here explain every move in that calculation.
The order to read it in

items: Density Matrices and Channels (#/qrc/open-systems/density-matrices-and-channels) (about two to three hours). The state of a reservoir is a density matrix and every input step is a channel. You build the density matrix from ensembles, expand it in Pauli operators (the coordinates that the readout sees), learn the partial trace, and meet channels in four forms: Kraus operators, an environment you trace out, the Choi matrix, and the Pauli transfer matrix (for a qubit, an affine map of the Bloch ball). The page ends with the reset channel that writes the input and with a complete reservoir step worked with numbers.

Lindblad Dynamics (#/qrc/open-systems/lindblad-dynamics) (about two hours). Channels in continuous time: the Lindblad master equation, derived from a short-time Kraus channel. You solve it for a qubit (T1 and T2), turn it into a matrix whose eigenvalues are relaxation rates, find steady states, convert a rate into the damping of one reservoir step, and meet quantum trajectories.

Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points) (about two to three hours). The trace distance between states, the fact that channels never increase it, the contraction coefficient of a channel, fixed points and the spectrum of a channel, conserved quantities that break forgetting, and the sufficient condition for the echo state property. A widget and a code sample show two copies of a reservoir converging, or failing to.

Measurement (#/qrc/open-systems/measurement) (about two hours). General measurements (POVMs), what a discarded measurement does to the state, shot noise and how many shots a feature vector needs, which observables share shots, back-action on time series, and weak measurement as a dial between information and disturbance.

blocks.text: Read them in this order: the second and third both lean on the first, and the fourth uses the idea from the first that a measurement is a channel. If you are short of time, the density matrix, partial trace, Kraus form and Bloch map of the first page, the T1 and T2 section of the second, and the trace distance and contraction coefficient of the third are the parts the Models shelf uses most. The whole chapter takes about nine hours with the exercises.
These five statements carry the chapter. Each is derived in full on the page named.

blocks.caption: A state is its list of Pauli expectation values; a readout sees a few of them. Page: Density Matrices and Channels.
A channel in Kraus form: the input step of a reservoir. For one qubit it acts on the Bloch vector as $\vec r\mapsto T\vec r+\vec t$. Page: Density Matrices and Channels.
The Lindblad equation: a Hamiltonian part plus jump operators. Its slowest decay rate (the gap) sets the memory time. Page: Lindblad Dynamics.
Contraction of the trace distance: if every input channel has $\eta\le1-\epsilon$, two initial states are forgotten as $(1-\epsilon)^k$. Page: Contraction and Fixed Points.
Shots needed to estimate $M$ features to accuracy $\epsilon$ with confidence $1-\delta$. Page: Measurement.

blocks.text: The thread through the chapter is one picture of a reservoir step. The data $s_k$ chooses a channel $\mathcal T_{s_k}$, built from a reset that writes the input and a unitary that mixes it into the other qubits. The state after $k$ steps is the composition of these channels applied to the initial state. Whether the reservoir forgets that initial state is a question about the contraction of the composition (third page). How fast it forgets in continuous time is a question about the spectrum of a Liouvillian (second page). What the readout gets is a set of expectation values $\operatorname{Tr}(O\rho)$ (first page) estimated from shots that disturb the state (fourth page).
How this connects to the rest of the shelf

items: The Fujii-Nakajima spin reservoir of The Spin-Network Reservoir (#/qrc/models/spin-network-reservoir) is exactly 'reset one qubit (a channel), then evolve unitarily': its memory comes entirely from the reset.

Whether that is enough to forget depends on the Hamiltonian: Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes) shows that conserved quantities (integrable or localised regimes) spoil it, which is the fixed-point story of the third page.
Added dissipation (Dissipation as a Resource (#/qrc/models/dissipation-as-resource)) and natural hardware noise turn the T1 and T2 physics of the second page into a tuning knob.

Measurement back-action and shot noise (Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action), Resource Accounting (#/qrc/hardware/resource-accounting)) set the real cost of running any of this, following the fourth page.
On the Theory shelf, Concentration and Scalability (#/qrc/theory/concentration-and-scalability) asks how the number of shots must grow with the number of qubits.

blocks.text: What you will be able to do afterwards

items: Write the state of a partly mixed reservoir as a density matrix, read its Pauli coordinates and trace out any subset of qubits.
Take any proposed map, test whether it is a physical channel, and say what it does to the Bloch ball.
Convert T1 and T2 into the per-step noise of a reservoir and into a memory length measured in input steps.
Decide whether a given reservoir has fading memory, estimate how long its washout must be, and find the symmetry that spoils it if not.
Budget the shots and measurement settings of an experiment, and weigh weak against projective readout.
